spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players using data on 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain) in the 2012-2013 season

the adjusted risk difference for red cards (dark vs light skin) is 0.232 percentage points, 95% CI [0.020, 0.444], p=0.032, after adjusting for games, position, league country, height, weight and yellow cards
the adjusted odds ratio for red cards (dark vs light skin) is 1.20, 95% CI [1.025, 1.406], p=0.023
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to red-card dark-skinned players is concluded to be supported, since the risk-difference CI excludes zero at α=0.05
the effect is described as modest in absolute terms (0.23 percentage points) but as a meaningful 19% relative increase in red-card probability for dark-skinned players
the source data comprises 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European leagues in 2012-2013, including 2,053 players and 3,147 referees
two independent raters coded player skin tone from profile photos on a 5-point scale
the inter-rater correlation for skin tone coding was found to be 0.923, described as excellent agreement
the two raters' skin tone scores were averaged for use in the analysis
the unit of analysis was chosen to be the player-referee dyad rather than individual matches
the final analytic sample was N=99,645 dyads, comprising 83,655 light-skin and 15,990 dark-skin dyads
38,423 dyads with intermediate skin tone (0.25–0.75) were excluded to maximize contrast between groups
7,960 dyads were excluded due to missing covariate data, primarily missing position
there were 1,241 total red card incidents, 1.25% of dyads

extreme skin-tone categories (≤0.25 light vs ≥0.75 dark) were used, justified by maximizing contrast, aligning with the research question, avoiding ambiguity, and matching the original scale's framing
a median split or continuous skin-tone measure was rejected in favor of the extreme-category approach
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of any red card in the dyad
the primary exposure was defined as dark skin (1) versus light skin (0)
a logistic regression was fit with the specified formula including darkSkin, games, position, leagueCountry, height, weight and yellowCards
games (continuous) was included as a covariate to control for exposure/opportunity
position (12 categories, reference Attacking Midfielder) was included as a covariate
leagueCountry (4 categories, reference England) was included as a covariate
height (continuous) was included as a covariate
weight (continuous) was included as a covariate
yellowCards (continuous) was included as a covariate to proxy aggressive playing style

spans.note: justification narrative explaining why each covariate was chosen (exposure control, physicality, league culture, aggression proxy)

spans.assertion: the fitted model had N=99,645, Pseudo R²=0.0755, log-likelihood=-6,171.84, and converged successfully

spans.note: Estimation Method for Risk Difference heading

spans.assertion: the risk difference was computed via marginal standardization/G-computation: fitting the model, creating counterfactual all-dark and all-light datasets, predicting probabilities under each, and differencing the mean predictions

spans.note: Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals subheading

spans.assertion: the delta method (with a chain-rule gradient) was used to compute the SE of the risk difference, the 95% CI was formed as RD±1.96×SE, and a two-sided Wald test was used for H0: RD=0
descriptive statistics (mean/SD) for games, height, weight, yellow cards, and red card rate are reported separately for light-skin and dark-skin groups
light-skinned players have slightly more games on average (3.08 vs 2.98)
light-skinned players are slightly taller on average (182.4 vs 181.6 cm)
yellow card rates are similar between the two skin-tone groups
unadjusted red card rates are 1.21% for light-skinned and 1.41% for dark-skinned players

dark-skinned players are more concentrated in forward positions (23.5% vs 12.4% Center Forward) and less in goalkeeper/attacking-midfielder roles, while light-skinned players are more common in defensive positions like center back
dark-skinned players are more common in the English and French leagues while light-skinned players are more common in the German and Spanish leagues
unadjusted red card rates were 1.2145% (light) and 1.4071% (dark), an unadjusted risk difference of 0.193 percentage points
the unadjusted odds ratio was 1.161, 95% CI [1.004, 1.343], p=0.044
adjusted risk was 1.4405% for dark skin and 1.2089% for light skin, giving an adjusted risk difference of 0.232 percentage points
the risk difference has SE=0.108pp, 95% CI [0.020, 0.444]pp, z=2.14, two-sided p=0.032
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a 0.232 percentage point (0.0023 absolute) higher red-card chance than light-skinned players, a 19.2% relative increase over the 1.21% baseline
the adjusted effect is statistically significant at the α=0.05 level

spans.assertion: cumulative red card counts aggregated across all encounters in a dyad were used
individual match-level red card data was not used

spans.note: cannot assess temporal dynamics or learning effects
rare outcome (1.25% of dyads) creates statistical power limitations
yellow cards only partially capture playing-style/aggression confounding

spans.assertion: individual referee characteristics (age, experience, nationality) were not available/included; only country-level measures were used
match context variables (game importance, score differential, home/away status) were not available and not included
player club/team effects were not controlled for
player reputation/history known to referees was not controlled for
players without photos (14.7% of dyads) were excluded from the analysis

spans.note: excluding intermediate skin tones means the effect may differ across the full distribution
survival bias inherent to dyad structure — only encounters that occurred are included

spans.assertion: reverse causation was deemed not applicable because skin tone is fixed and precedes referee decisions

spans.note: four unresolved alternative explanations offered for the association: positional confounding, league-specific effects, differential opportunity, and referee stereotyping
Statistical Assumptions / Logistic Regression Assumptions heading

spans.assertion: the log-linearity assumption for continuous covariates may not hold, particularly for games, which shows a non-linear pattern
non-independence among dyads sharing the same player or referee was not accounted for (no clustering adjustment), which may underestimate standard errors
variance inflation factors were checked for multicollinearity between position and skin tone and found acceptable
interaction terms (e.g., skin tone × position or × league) were not included in the model

spans.note: Sample Size for Rare Outcomes subheading

spans.assertion: there are only 1,241 red cards across 99,645 observations
most covariates have sufficient variation, but some position categories are small

spans.note: findings specific to European professional soccer, 2012-2013 season
findings may not generalize to other time periods, leagues/countries, amateur/youth soccer, or other sports
player population is elite professional athletes; dynamics may differ elsewhere

spans.assertion: the large sample size (~100,000 dyads) provides adequate statistical power
exposure measurement is high quality, with excellent inter-rater reliability (r=0.923)
comprehensive covariate adjustment was performed, controlling for exposure, position, league, physical characteristics, and playing style
marginal standardization was used as the method because it provides an interpretable risk difference on the probability scale
a sensitivity analysis incorporating referee country-level bias measures was conducted
results were found to be robust to inclusion of referee country-level bias measures
logistic regression was chosen as suitable for the binary/rare red-card outcome
aggregated dyad-level data was used rather than player-level data

spans.note: restatement of the primary research question

spans.assertion: the answer to the primary question is stated as SUPPORTED
statistically significant evidence was found that dark-skinned players receive red cards at a higher rate than light-skinned players even after adjustment
the adjusted risk difference is restated as 0.232 percentage points (95% CI [0.020, 0.444], p=0.032)
dark-skinned players have an absolute red card probability of 1.44% compared to 1.21% for light-skinned players
this represents a 19% relative increase in red card probability
in practical terms, approximately 2 additional red cards per 1,000 dyads are attributed to dark skin versus light skin
the 95% confidence interval excludes zero, indicating statistical significance at α=0.05
the adjusted odds ratio is restated as 1.20 (95% CI [1.025, 1.406], p=0.023)
the odds of a red card are 20% higher for dark-skinned players
the odds ratio result is consistent with the risk difference estimate
both estimands are statistically significant at α=0.05, and the risk-difference p-value of 0.032 allows rejecting the null hypothesis of no group difference

spans.note: transitional statement that the modest effect size is still meaningful in context
general background fact that red cards are rare but consequential events

spans.assertion: the effect persists after controlling for legitimate differences (position, playing style, exposure)
the 19% relative increase is interpreted as representing systematic differential treatment

spans.assertion: the final conclusion states the hypothesis is supported: the adjusted risk difference of 0.23 percentage points is statistically significant (p=0.032), robust to sensitivity analyses, and represents compelling if modest evidence of differential treatment
